respStmt.resp: traduction anglaise depuis le grec (zoo7/7g), verification humaine requise

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale et complete produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo7/7g.xml (edition Bekker, Open Greek and Latin / First1000Years of Greek, CC BY-SA 4.0), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Le decoupage en 178 chapitres et en sections numerotees suit exactement la structure TEI de la source (chaque section source correspond a un paragraphe de cette traduction, 224 sections au total) ; les titres de chapitres sont fournis par le traducteur pour la lisibilite, le texte grec n'en comportant pas. Il s'agit d'un recueil paradoxographique melangeant faits zoologiques, botaniques, mineralogiques, geographiques et historiques ; traduit ici dans son integralite comme une oeuvre unique et coherente, conformement au traitement deja applique aux autres textes paradoxographiques courts du corpus.

div.head: The bolinthos of Paeonia
div.p: In Paeonia, on the mountain called Hesaenus, which marks the boundary between Paeonia and Maedica, they say there is a beast called the bolinthos, and by the Paeonians the monaepos.

They say this creature is in its general nature very like an ox, but differs in size and strength, and further in its mane; for it has, hanging from the neck like a horse's, a mane that is very deep, running from the crown of the head down to the eyes.

Its horns are not like those of oxen, but bent back, with the point turned down beside the ears; each of them holds more than half a jar, and they are very black, and gleam as though polished. When the hide is flayed off, it can cover a couch fit for eight. When it is struck, it flees, and if it is unable to flee, it stands its ground.

Its flesh is sweet to eat. It defends itself by kicking and by voiding its dung behind it, to a distance of about four fathoms; it does this readily and often, and the dung so scorches that it strips the hair from dogs.

They say it does this when disturbed, but does not scorch when undisturbed. When they give birth, the largest of them gather together in a group and give birth all at once, voiding their dung in a circle around themselves; for the beast discharges a great quantity of this excrement.

div.head: The camels of Arabia
div.p: They say the camels in Arabia will not mount their mothers, and even if one is forced to it, they are unwilling. Indeed, it is said that once, there being no other stallion available, the keeper covered the mother and let the young male in unknowing. When he had mounted, thinking he was covering another, he completed the act; but a little later, on realizing what he had done, he bit and killed the camel-keeper.

div.head: The cuckoo of Helice
div.p: They say that the cuckoos at Helice, when about to lay, do not build a nest, but lay their eggs in the nests of ring-doves or turtle-doves, and neither brood nor hatch nor rear the young themselves; but when the chick is born and grown, it drives out of the nest those with whom it had been reared. It grows, it seems, large and handsome, so that it easily overpowers the rest. And they say the doves take such pleasure in it that they themselves join in driving out their own chicks along with it.

div.head: The goats of Crete and dittany
div.p: The goats in Crete, when shot with an arrow, seek out, it seems, the dittany that grows there; for as soon as they eat it, they at once expel the arrow.

div.head: The deer of Achaea and their shed antlers
div.p: They say that certain of the deer in Achaea, when they shed their antlers, go off to places where they cannot easily be found. They do this because they have nothing left to defend themselves with, and because the places from which the antlers fell are sore; and on many of them ivy is seen to have grown in the place where the antlers were.

div.head: The leopard-drug of Armenia
div.p: In Armenia they say there grows a certain drug called "leopard's-bane." With this, whenever a leopard is sighted, they smear a sacrificial animal and let it loose. The leopard, when it touches the animal, then seeks out, it seems, human dung; wherefore the hunters put such dung into a vessel and hang it from a tree, so that the leopard, leaping up after it again and again and becoming exhausted, is overcome by it and falls into their hands.

div.head: The plover and the crocodile
div.p: In Egypt they say the plovers fly into the mouths of crocodiles and clean their teeth, drawing out the bits of flesh caught in their jaws; and the crocodiles are pleased by this and do the birds no harm.

div.head: The hedgehogs of Byzantium
div.p: They say the hedgehogs at Byzantium perceive when the wind is blowing from the north or from the south, and change their burrows accordingly at once: when the wind is southerly, they make their burrows facing the ground, and when northerly, facing the walls.

div.head: The goats of Cephallenia
div.p: The goats in Cephallenia do not drink, it seems, as the other four-footed creatures do, but every day they turn their faces toward the sea and stand gaping, taking in the breezes.

div.head: The wild asses of Syria
div.p: They say that among the wild asses of Syria, one leads the herd, and whenever one of the younger colts mounts a female, the leader grows enraged and pursues him until he catches him, and, stooping over his hindquarters, tears off his genitals with his mouth.

div.head: The tortoise and marjoram
div.p: They say that tortoises, when they have eaten a viper, eat marjoram afterward, and if they cannot find it quickly enough, they die. Many countryfolk, wishing to test whether this is true, pluck away the marjoram whenever they see a tortoise doing this; and when they do so, the tortoise is soon after seen to die.

div.head: The polecat's member
div.p: The polecat's member is said to be unlike that of other animals in nature, but solid throughout, like a bone, whatever state the animal may be in. They say it is among the best remedies for strangury, and is given scraped into powder.

div.head: The woodpecker
div.p: They say the woodpecker walks upon trees as lizards do, both upright and upon its belly. It is said to feed on the grubs found in trees, and to dig into the trees so deeply in search of these grubs that it can bring the trees down.

div.head: The pelican
div.p: They say the pelicans dig up and swallow the mussels found in rivers, and then, when they have taken in a great quantity of them, vomit them up, and so eat the flesh of the mussels, without touching the shells.

div.head: The white blackbirds of Cyllene
div.p: They say that at Cyllene in Arcadia the blackbirds are white, and nowhere else, and utter varied cries. They fly out toward the moon; but if one attempts to hunt them by day, they are very difficult to catch.

div.head: The short-lived honey of Melos and Cnidus
div.p: It is said by some that the honey called "flower-honey," found about Melos and Cnidus, is fragrant in scent but short-lived, and that the substance called eritháke (bee-bread) also occurs in it.

div.head: Honey without honeycomb in Cappadocia
div.p: About Cappadocia, in certain places, they say honey is produced without honeycombs, and comes out with a thickness like that of olive oil.

div.head: The heavy-scented honey of Trapezus
div.p: At Trapezus on the Black Sea there is produced a heavy-scented honey from the box-tree; and they say that this drives the healthy out of their senses, but wholly cures those subject to epileptic fits.

div.head: Honey-cakes of Lydia and Thrace
div.p: They say that in Lydia too much honey is gathered from the trees, and the inhabitants make cakes from it without wax, cutting it and using it after further working. It occurs also in Thrace, though not so solid there, but rather sandy in texture. They say all honey, when it solidifies, keeps the same volume, unlike water and the other liquids.

div.head: Chalcidian grass and almonds for bee-keeping
div.p: Chalcidian grass and almonds are most useful for making honey; for they say the greatest yield of brood comes from them.

div.head: Bees and perfume
div.p: They say bees are stupefied by perfume and cannot bear the scent; and some say that they attack most fiercely those who have anointed themselves with it.

div.head: Wine made from honey among the Taulantii
div.p: Among the Illyrians they say the people called Taulantii make wine from honey. When they have pressed out the honeycombs, they pour on water and boil it in a cauldron until half of it boils away, then pour it into jars, and, having reduced it to half its bulk, set it upon boards; there, they say, it ferments for a long time and becomes wine-like, pleasant, and full-bodied. They say this has already happened, too, to some in Greece, so that it was in no way different from old wine; and those who later sought to reproduce the blend could not discover it.

div.head: The snakes and storks of Thessaly
div.p: About Thessaly they record that so great a number of snakes were once born alive that, had the storks not destroyed them, the people would have had to abandon the land. For this reason they honour the storks, and it is not lawful to kill one; and if anyone does, he becomes liable to the same penalties as a murderer.

div.head: The Spartans and their snake-plague
div.p: Likewise it is recorded that at Lacedaemon, at a certain time, there arose so great a multitude of snakes that the Spartans, through scarcity of food, made use of them for nourishment; whence the Pythia is said to have addressed them as "snake-necked."

div.head: The iron-eating mice of Cyprus
div.p: On the island of Cyprus it is said that the mice eat iron.

div.head: The Chalybes and their gold
div.p: They say too that the Chalybes gather gold, brought together from many sources, on a small island lying above their territory; wherefore, it seems, they also disembowel those found working in the mines.

div.head: The scorpions on the road to Media
div.p: It is said that, on the road from Susa to Media, at the second stopping-place, there occurs an immense multitude of scorpions. Wherefore the King of the Persians, whenever he passed that way, would remain three days, ordering all his men to hunt them down; and to whoever caught the most he would give a prize.

div.head: The many kinds of mice at Cyrene
div.p: At Cyrene they say there is not a single kind of mouse, but many, differing both in form and colour; for some, they say, are flat-faced, like weasels, and some are hedgehog-like, which they call "hedgehog-mice."

div.head: The revivifying pool of Cilicia
div.p: About Cilicia they say there is a small gathering of water, into which, when drowned birds and other animals are dipped, they come back to life.

div.head: The colour-changing tarandos of Scythia
div.p: Among the Scythians called Gelonians they say a beast occurs, exceedingly rare, called the tarandos; it is said to change the colour of its hair according to whatever place it happens to be in.

For this reason it is hard to hunt, both for its speed and because of this change; for it takes on the colour, whether of trees or of any other surroundings, of whatever it is among. Most remarkable of all is that it changes its hair itself; the rest, such as the chameleon and the octopus, change only the skin. In size it is about as large as an ox, and the shape of its face is like that of a deer.

div.head: The madman of Abydos and the theatre
div.p: It is said that a certain man at Abydos, deranged in mind, went to the theatre for many days and watched as though actors were performing, and applauded; and that when he was restored from his derangement, he said that of all the time of his life, that had been the most pleasant.

div.head: The wine-seller of Tarentum
div.p: And at Tarentum they say a certain wine-seller was mad by night but sold wine by day, and yet he kept the key of his shop fastened at his belt, and, though many tried to steal it away from him, he never once lost it.

div.head: The fire-stones of Tenos and Bithynia
div.p: On the island of Tenos they say there is a small vessel of mixed material from which fire is kindled very easily. And in Bithynia, in Thrace, there occurs in the mines the stone called spinos, from which too they say fire is kindled.

div.head: The natural oven of Lipara
div.p: At Lipara they say there is a certain vent of hot air, in which, if a pot is hidden with whatever one wishes placed inside, it will cook.

div.head: The fires of Media and Persia
div.p: There are also, in Media and in Psittacene in Persia, fires that burn continually: that in Media is small, but that in Psittacene is great and burns with a clear flame; wherefore the King of the Persians even built kitchens beside it. Both are in level ground, not on heights. These are visible both by night and by day, but those about Pamphylia only by night.

div.head: The oil-fed flame near Apollonia
div.p: They say too that near Apollonia, on the borders of the territory of Apollonia, there is a certain rock from which the rising fire is not visible, but when oil is poured upon it, it bursts into flame.

div.head: Fires beyond the Pillars of Heracles
div.p: It is said too that fires burn beyond the Pillars of Heracles, some continually, some only by night, as the voyage of Hanno relates. That at Lipara too is visible and flame-like, but not by day, only by night. And they say there is also at Pithecusae something exceedingly fiery and hot, though not actually burning.

div.head: The intermittent fire of Lipara; the flow of Etna
div.p: Xenophanes says that the fire at Lipara once even died out for sixteen years, and returned in the seventeenth. The flow at Etna, they say, is neither flame-like nor continuous, but occurs only after many years.

div.head: The great fire of Lydia
div.p: It is said that about Lydia too a very great fire once boiled up, and burned for seven days.

div.head: The great fire-flow of Sicily
div.p: A remarkable thing occurs in Sicily concerning the fiery flow: the breadth of the boiling-up of the fire is forty stades, and the height to which it is borne, three.

div.head: The burning stone of Thrace
div.p: They say the stone called spinos in Thrace, when broken up, burns, and, when gathered back together, burns again, like charcoal-dust, when sprinkled with water. The stone called marieus does the same.

div.head: The self-growing gold of Philippi
div.p: About Philippi in Macedonia they say there are mines from which the tailings that are cast out are said to grow and produce gold, and that this is plainly visible.

div.head: The growing copper of Cyprus
div.p: They say too that near Tyrrhias in Cyprus a similar copper occurs. For, it seems, they cut it into small pieces and sow it; then, when rains come, it grows and puts forth shoots, and is thus gathered in.

div.head: The self-refilling quarries of Melos
div.p: They say too that on the island of Melos, in the places dug out, refillings occur again in the earth.

div.head: Unsmelted gold in Paeonia
div.p: About Paeonia they say that when there are continuous rains, gold called "unfired" gold is found as the earth is washed away. They say the earth in Paeonia is so rich in gold that many have found lumps weighing over a mina. They say a certain man found two lumps and brought them to the king, one weighing three minas, the other five; these, they say, lie beside the king's table, and from these first, whenever he eats anything, he makes his offering.

div.head: Gold-bearing rivers of Bactria and Iberia
div.p: They say too that in Bactria the river Oxus carries down a great abundance of gold nuggets, and that in Iberia the river called Theodorus casts up much gold about its banks, and likewise carries it down.

div.head: Buried gold in Pieria
div.p: They say too that in Pieria in Macedonia unwrought gold was buried by the ancient kings, and that, of four chasms there, gold as large as a span grew up out of one of them.

div.head: Chalybian and Amisene iron
div.p: The origin of Chalybian and Amisene iron is said to be quite peculiar. It forms, they say, from the sand carried down by the rivers. Some say they simply wash this and smelt it in the furnace; others say the residue formed from the washing, after being washed many times, is burned together with the addition of the so-called "fire-resisting stone," which is abundant in that country. This iron is far finer than any other. Had it not been smelted in a single furnace, it seems it would have been no different from silver. They say it alone does not rust, though little of it is produced.

div.head: The bright, rustless bronze of India
div.p: They say too that among the Indians bronze is so bright and pure and rustless that it cannot be told apart by its colour from gold; and among Darius's drinking-vessels there were several bowls of it, which could only be distinguished from gold ones by their smell.

div.head: Celtic tin
div.p: Celtic tin, they say, melts much faster than lead. A sign of how readily it melts is that it seems even to melt in water; at any rate, it stains quickly, it seems. It melts too in the cold, once it has frozen, the heat naturally within it being, as they say, shut in and driven inward on account of its weakness.

div.head: The sacred olive of the Pantheum
div.p: In the Pantheum there is an olive tree called "of the fair garland." All the leaves of this tree are the reverse of other olive trees': they have their pale green side outward, not inward. It sends out shoots suitable for garlands, in due measure, like the myrtle. Heracles, taking a cutting from this tree, planted it at Olympia, and from it are given the crowns awarded to the athletes. This tree stands beside the river Lissus, sixty stades from the river, and is walled about, and there is a heavy penalty for touching it. From it the Eleans took a cutting and planted it at Olympia, and from it they give the victors' crowns.

div.head: The petrified vessels in the Lydian mines
div.p: In the mines of Lydia near Pergamon, which Croesus once worked, a war broke out and those working the mines took refuge in them; the entrance being then walled up, they were suffocated. Long afterward, when the mines were cleared out, the vessels they had used for their daily needs were found turned to stone, amphorae and the like. These vessels, filled with whatever liquid had been in them, had turned to stone, and so too had the bones of the men.

div.head: The soap-like water of Lake Ascania
div.p: The water of Lake Ascania is so full of nitre that clothes need no other cleansing agent; and if one leaves them in the water too long, they fall apart.

div.head: The wells of Pythopolis
div.p: Near Lake Ascania is a village called Pythopolis, about a hundred and twenty stades from Cius, in which, in winter, all the wells dry up so completely that a vessel cannot be dipped in them, but in summer they fill right to the brim.

div.head: The strait of Sicily and the moon
div.p: The strait between Sicily and Italy waxes and wanes together with the moon.

div.head: The spring near Syracuse
div.p: And on the road to Syracuse there is a spring in a meadow, neither large nor holding much water; but when a great crowd once gathered there together, it provided water in abundance.

div.head: The oath-spring of the Palici
div.p: There is also a spring at the place called Palici in Sicily, holding about as much as would serve ten couches; this spring throws up water to a height of six cubits, so that onlookers think the plain is about to be flooded, and then it settles back to the same level again. There is also an oath there, held to be sacred: whatever oath a man swears, he writes it upon a little tablet and casts it into the water.

If, then, he swears truly, the tablet floats on the surface; but if he swears falsely, the tablet, they say, grows heavy and disappears, and the man himself is burned. Wherefore the priest takes securities from him beforehand, for the purifying of the shrine.

div.head: Demonesos and its mines
div.p: Demonesos, the island of the Carthaginians, took its name from Demonesos, who first worked it; the place has a mine of blue pigment and of chrysocolla. The finest of this finds a price equal to gold, for it is also a remedy for the eyes.

There is also there a copper that can be worked underwater, at a depth of two fathoms; whence come the statue at Sicyon in the ancient temple of Apollo, and those at Pheneus called "mountain-bronze." They are inscribed: "Heracles, son of Amphitryon, dedicated this, having taken Elis."

He took Elis under the guidance, according to an oracle, of a woman whose father, Augeas, he had killed. Those who mine this copper become exceedingly sharp-sighted, and those without eyelashes grow them; wherefore physicians use the flower of copper and Phrygian ash for the eyes.

div.head: The dripping cave of Demonesos
div.p: There is also, there, a cave called "the hollow one"; in it, columns have formed, hardened from certain dripping waters. This is shown clearly where it narrows toward the floor, for it is narrowest there.

div.head: The lineage of the eagles and vultures
div.p: Of the pair of eagles, one of their offspring becomes, in alternation, an osprey, until a mated pair of these results. From ospreys comes the sea-eagle; from these, the dusky vultures and the griffon vultures; and these last no longer produce distinct kinds among the vultures, but breed the great vultures, which are barren. A sign of this is that no one has ever seen the nest of a great vulture.

div.head: Indian lead and cold water
div.p: A remarkable thing, they say, occurs among the Indians concerning the lead there: when it is melted and poured into cold water, it leaps out of the water.

div.head: The Mossynoecian bronze
div.p: They say the bronze of the Mossynoeci is the brightest and whitest, tin not being mixed with it, but a certain earth of its own being smelted together with it. They say the man who discovered the blend taught it to no one; wherefore the bronze vessels made there in earlier times are of a different quality from those made since.

div.head: The birds and fish insensible to fire
div.p: In the region of the Black Sea they say a certain bird is found in winter, hibernating, neither voiding excrement nor feeling anything when its feathers are plucked, nor even when it is set upon the spit, but only when it is scorched by the fire. They say many fish, too, when cut and sliced, feel nothing, but only when they are heated through by the fire.

div.head: The bee and the solstice
div.p: The bee seems to signal the solstices by going out to work, which is the sign the bee-keepers use, since they become quiet at that time. The cicadas too seem to sing after the solstice.

div.head: The fasting hedgehog
div.p: They say too that the hedgehog can go without food for as much as a year.

div.head: The gecko's shed skin
div.p: They say that the gecko, when it sheds its skin as snakes do, turns and swallows it; physicians watch for this, since it is useful for those subject to epilepsy.

div.head: The swelling fat of the hibernating bear
div.p: They say too that the fat of the bear, when it has congealed through the winter cold during the time the bear is hibernating, grows and swells beyond the vessels that contain it.

div.head: The voiceless frogs of Cyrene; the solid-hoofed swine of Macedonia
div.p: At Cyrene they say the frogs there are altogether voiceless. And in Macedonia, in the territory of the Emathiotae, the swine are solid-hoofed.

div.head: Fertile mules in Cappadocia; fruit-bearing black poplars in Crete
div.p: In Cappadocia they say mules are fertile, and in Crete black poplars bear fruit.

div.head: The silent frogs of Seriphus
div.p: They say too that at Seriphus the frogs do not sing; but if they are carried to another place, they do sing.

div.head: The wandering fish of India
div.p: Among the Indians, in the place called "the Horn," they say there occur little fish that wander about on dry land and then run back again into the river.

div.head: The land-walking fish of Babylon
div.p: Some say too that near Babylon certain fish remain in the burrows that hold moisture when the river dries up; that these come out and graze upon the threshing-floors, walking on their fins and waving their tails; and that when pursued, they flee, and, having slipped into their holes, turn to face their pursuer; for often men approach and provoke them. They have a head like that of a sea-frog, but the rest of the body like a goby's, and gills like other fish.

div.head: The dug-up fish of Heraclea and Rhegium
div.p: At Heraclea on the Black Sea, and at Rhegium, they say fish are dug up out of the ground, especially in riverside and marshy places. It happens that when these places dry up at certain times, the fish withdraw into the earth, and, as it dries further, follow the moisture deeper into the soil, and then, when it is dry, remain within the dampness, as creatures in their burrows survive; and when the ground is dug up before the water returns, they are then found to move.

div.head: The excellent buried fish of Paphlagonia
div.p: They say too that about Paphlagonia dug-up fish occur at depth, and that these are of excellent quality, though there is no visible water nearby, nor rivers flowing in, but the earth itself gives them life.

div.head: The buried right antler of the deer of Epirus
div.p: They say the deer in Epirus bury their right antler when they shed it, and that it is useful for many purposes.

div.head: The lynx and its urine
div.p: They say too that the lynx covers over its urine, because it is useful for other purposes and especially for engraved gems.

div.head: The seal's rennet
div.p: They say too that the seal vomits up its rennet when it is caught, and that this is medicinal and useful for those subject to epilepsy.

div.head: The deadly poison of Mount Circaeum
div.p: It is said that about Italy, on Mount Circaeum, there grows a certain deadly poison, of such power that if it is sprinkled on anyone, it at once makes him fall, causes the hair on his body to drop out, and makes the limbs of the whole body waste away, so that the appearance of those dying of it is pitiable. They say Aulus Peucetius and Gaius, about to give this to Cleonymus the Spartan, were discovered, and, upon investigation by the Tarentines, put to death.

div.head: The sacred birds of Diomedes' island
div.p: On the island of Diomedeia, which lies in the Adriatic, they say there is a shrine of Diomedes, wondrous and holy, and that around the shrine, in a circle, sit birds of great size, with large, hard beaks.

They say that if Greeks land at the place, these birds keep still; but if any of the surrounding barbarians land, the birds fly up and, hovering, hurl themselves down upon their heads, and, wounding them with their beaks, kill them.

The myth is that these birds arose from the companions of Diomedes, who were shipwrecked about the island when Diomedes himself was treacherously murdered by Aeneas, who had then become king of those parts.

div.head: The prolific livestock and women of Umbria
div.p: Among the Umbrians they say the livestock give birth three times a year, and the earth yields crops many times what is sown; the women too, they say, bear many children, and rarely bear only one, but most bear two or three.

div.head: The Electrid islands, Daedalus, and amber
div.p: In the Electrid islands, which lie in the recess of the Adriatic, they say there stand two statues dedicated there, one of tin and one of bronze, worked in the ancient manner. These are said to be the work of Daedalus, a memorial of ancient times, when, fleeing Minos from Sicily and Crete, he put in at these places,

They say these islands were formed by the silting of the river Eridanus. There is also, it seems, a lake near the river, holding hot water; a heavy and noxious smell rises from it, and no animal drinks from it, nor does any bird fly over it, but falls and dies. Its circumference is two hundred stades, its width about ten.

The local people tell the myth that Phaethon, struck by the thunderbolt, fell into this lake. They say there are many black poplars in it, from which falls the substance called amber. This, they say, is like gum, hardening like a stone, and is gathered by the local people and carried to the Greeks.

To these islands, then, they say Daedalus came, and, taking possession of them, set up his own image on one of them, and that of his son Icarus on the other. Later, when the Pelasgians, driven out of Argos, sailed against them, Daedalus fled, and came to the island of Icarus.

div.head: The cave of Enna and the fields of Persephone
div.p: In Sicily, near the place called Enna, they say there is a certain cave, around which there grows, in a circle, a great abundance of flowers of every season, but especially of violets, filling an unbounded space, which fills the surrounding country with fragrance, so that hunters, whose dogs are overcome by the scent, are unable to track the hares.

Through this chasm there runs, it is said, a hidden underground passage, through which they say Pluto carried off Persephone. They say wheat is found in this place unlike either that used by the local people or any imported kind, but possessing some great peculiarity of its own; and by this they infer that grain first appeared among them there. Wherefore they lay claim to Demeter too, saying the goddess was born among them.

div.head: The absence of wolves, bears, and vipers in Crete
div.p: They say that wolves, bears, and vipers, and likewise beasts resembling these, do not occur in Crete, because Zeus was born there.

div.head: The forbidden fertile island beyond the Pillars of Heracles
div.p: In the sea outside the Pillars of Heracles they say an uninhabited island was discovered by the Carthaginians, having forests of every kind and navigable rivers, and marvellous in its other produce, a voyage of several days away; and that when the Carthaginians used to visit it often, on account of its fertility, some even settling there, the leading men of Carthage proclaimed that they would punish with death any who sailed to it, and destroyed all the settlers, lest word should spread and a great multitude, gathering against them, should seize the island for themselves and take away the prosperity of the Carthaginians.

div.head: The protected Heraclean road
div.p: They say there is a road, called the Heraclean road, running from Italy to the land of the Celts, the Celtoligurians, and the Iberians, along which, whether a Greek or a native travels, he is watched over by those dwelling nearby, that he suffer no wrong; for the penalty is paid by whoever's territory the wrong occurs in.

div.head: The Celtic arrow-poison and its antidote
div.p: They say the Celts have a drug they call "toxikon," which is said to work destruction so swiftly that Celtic hunters, when they have shot a deer or some other animal with it, run up in haste and cut away the wounded flesh before the poison spreads, both for the sake of eating the meat and so that the animal should not putrefy.

They say an antidote for this has been discovered in the bark of the oak; others say a different leaf, which they call "raven's-leaf," because it was observed by them that a raven, having tasted the poison and being badly affected, rushed to this leaf, and, swallowing it, ceased its suffering.

div.head: The silver revealed by fire in Iberia
div.p: In Iberia they say that when certain shepherds set the woodlands ablaze, and the ground was heated by the burning, silver plainly flowed from the earth, and afterward, when earthquakes occurred and the ground split open, an immense quantity of silver was gathered, which brought the Massaliots no small revenue.

div.head: The Gymnesian islands: pine-resin oil and the effeminate Iberians
div.p: On the Gymnesian islands, which lie off Iberia, and which they say are counted next after the seven greatest islands, they say no oil is made from olives, but a great quantity, suited to every use, is made from the terebinth. They say the Iberians who live there are so given to women that they give traders four or five male slaves in exchange for a single female one.

When they serve as mercenaries among the Carthaginians and receive their pay, it seems they buy nothing else with it but women; for no one among them is allowed to possess gold or silver. It is said that this prohibition on bringing in money among them arose because Heracles made his expedition against Iberia on account of the wealth of its inhabitants.

div.head: The fish-teeming lake of the Massaliots
div.p: In the territory of the Massaliots, near Liguria, they say there is a certain lake, which boils up and overflows, casting out so vast a multitude of fish as to be scarcely believable. When the etesian winds blow, the ground silts up over it, and such a quantity of dust forms there that its surface becomes solid, like a floor. The local people, cutting through it with tridents, readily draw out as many fish from it as they wish.

div.head: The skilled Ligurian slingers
div.p: It is said that some of the Ligurians sling so well that, when they see a number of birds, they vie with one another over which bird each is to aim at, as though sure of hitting whichever they choose.

div.head: The Ligurian women who give birth while working
div.p: They say this too is peculiar to them: the women, while working, give birth, and, having washed the child in water, immediately go back to digging and hoeing and managing the other tasks they would have had to do even had they not given birth.

div.head: The rising river of Liguria
div.p: This too is a marvel among the Ligurians: they say there is among them a river whose current rises up and flows aloft, so that those on the far bank cannot be seen.

div.head: Copper and iron from the same mine in Tyrrhenia
div.p: In Tyrrhenia they say there is an island called Aethalia, in which, from the same mine, copper was formerly dug, from which, they say, all their implements were once made; then it could no longer be found, and after a long time iron appeared from the same mine, which the Tyrrhenians who inhabit the place called Populonium still use to this day.

div.head: The fortified city of Oenarea
div.p: There is a city in Tyrrhenia called Oenarea, said to be exceedingly well fortified; for in its midst there is a high hill, rising thirty stades, and below, forests of every kind and waters. The inhabitants, fearing that some tyrant might arise, are said to set over themselves as their leaders those freed from among their household slaves; these govern them, and each year others of the same kind are appointed in their place.

div.head: The Sibyl's chamber at Cumae; the petrifying river Cetus
div.p: At Cumae, near Italy, there is shown, it seems, an underground chamber of the Sibyl, the prophetess, who is said to have lived to a very great age and remained a virgin; she was an Erythraean, though called by some who dwell in Italy the Cumaean Sibyl, and by others Melancraera. This place is said to be held by the Lucanians.
They say too that in those places near Cumae there is a river called Cetus, into which whatever is first cast becomes, over time, coated round, and at last turns entirely to stone.

div.head: The costly robe of Alcimenes of Sybaris
div.p: They say a robe was made for Alcimenes the Sybarite of such extravagant costliness that it was displayed at the festival of Hera at Lacinium, to which all the people of Italy assemble, and that of all the things shown there, it was the most admired of all; Dionysius the Elder, having gained possession of it, is said to have sold it to the Carthaginians for a hundred and twenty talents.

It was of sea-purple, fifteen cubits in size, and was divided on either side with woven figures, the Susians above and the Persians below; and in the middle were Zeus, Hera, Themis, Athena, Apollo, and Aphrodite. At either end was Alcimenes himself, and on either side of him, Sybaris.

div.head: The blood-scented sea near Iapygia; Heracles' footprints
div.p: About the Iapygian headland they say that from a certain place, where, according to the myth, Heracles' battle with the giants took place, there flows a great quantity of ichor, so noxious that, on account of the heaviness of its smell, the sea in that region is unnavigable. They say there are, in many parts of Italy, many memorials of Heracles along the roads he travelled. About Pandosia in Iapygia, footprints of the god are shown, upon which no one may tread.

div.head: The finger-moved rock of Iapygia
div.p: There is also, about the Iapygian headland, a rock the size of a wagon, said to have been moved and set down there by Heracles; and it happens that it can be shifted by a single finger.

div.head: The fox, the dog, and the hidden passage at Orchomenus
div.p: In the city of the Orchomenians in Boeotia, they say a fox appeared, and, pursued by a dog, slipped into an underground passage, and the dog went in after it, and, barking, made a great echo, as though there were some open space there; the hunters, seized by a sudden inspiration, broke open the entrance and went in after them too; and, seeing light entering through certain openings, they were able to see the rest clearly, and, coming out, reported it to the magistrates.

div.head: The ancient works of Iolaus in Sardinia
div.p: On the island of Sardinia they say there are constructions arranged in the ancient Greek manner, many of them beautiful, including domed chambers carved with extraordinary patterns; these, they say, were built by Iolaus, son of Iphicles, when, taking with him the sons of Heracles by the daughters of Thespius, he sailed to those regions to settle them, as being, through their kinship with Heracles, entitled to them, since Heracles had become

master of the whole western region. This island, it seems, was formerly called Ichnussa, because its outline is very like a human footprint; it is said to have been prosperous and fruitful in every way in earlier times, for Aristaeus, said to have been the most skilled farmer of the ancients, is said in myth to have ruled over them, though formerly overrun by many great birds.

Now, however, it bears nothing of the kind, because, once subdued by the Carthaginians, all the crops useful for food were cut down, and the penalty of death was set for the inhabitants should anyone replant any such thing.

div.head: The haunted tomb on Lipara
div.p: On one of the seven islands called those of Aeolus, the one called Lipara, they tell a myth of a tomb, about which they say many other marvellous things, but all agree on this: that it is not safe to approach that place by night; for the sound of drums and cymbals is clearly heard, and laughter mixed with uproar, and rattles.

They tell of something still more marvellous that happened near the cave: a certain man, drunk, is said to have fallen asleep there before daybreak, and, sought by his household for three days, was found on the fourth as though dead and carried off by his kinsfolk to his own tomb; and, having received all the customary rites, he suddenly rose up, and told what had happened to him.
This seems to us rather too much like myth; nonetheless it seemed necessary not to leave it unmentioned, in composing this record of that place.

div.head: Lake Avernus and its clear waters
div.p: Near Cumae in Italy there is a lake called Avernus, which itself, it seems, has nothing remarkable about it; for they say hills surround it in a circle, no less than three stades in height, and it is itself circular in shape, of unfathomable depth.
But this seems remarkable: though thick trees overhang it, and some lean down over it, no leaf is ever seen resting on the water, but the water is so exceedingly clear that onlookers marvel at it.

Near the mainland close to it, not far off, hot water bursts out in many places, and the whole place is called Pyriphlegethon. That no bird flies over it is false; for those who have been there say a great number of swans occur upon it.

div.head: The Sirenusan islands
div.p: They say the Sirenusan islands lie in Italy about the strait, upon the headland itself, which lies before the place that juts forward and separates, with its bays, the gulf that surrounds Cumae from the one that encloses the place called Poseidonia; there too a temple of the Sirens is established, and they are honoured exceedingly by the surrounding people with careful sacrifices; and, remembering their names, they call them Parthenope, Leucosia, and the third, Ligeia.

div.head: Mount Delphion and the trading-post of the Mentores
div.p: It is said that between the land of the Mentores and Istria there is a mountain called Delphion, with a high peak. When the Mentores, who dwell on the Adriatic, climb this peak, they can, it seems, watch from afar the ships sailing into the Black Sea.

There is also, they say, a certain place among the intervening distances where a common market is held, and where the merchants coming up from the Black Sea sell Lesbian, Chian, and Thasian wares, and those from the Adriatic sell Corcyraean jars.

div.head: The Danube's two mouths and the voyage of the Argo
div.p: They say too that the Ister, flowing from the forests called Hercynian, splits, and flows in part into the Black Sea,

and in part empties into the Adriatic. We have observed a proof of this not only in recent times but even more among the ancients, in that those waters there are unnavigable; for they say Jason made his voyage in by way of the Cyanean rocks, and his voyage out from the Black Sea by way of the Ister; and they bring forward no few other proofs besides: in that country, they point to altars dedicated by Jason, and on one of the islands in the Adriatic, a shrine of Artemis founded by Medea.

They say too that he would not have sailed past the so-called Wandering Rocks, had he not been sailing out from there. And on the island of Aethalia, lying in the Tyrrhenian sea, they point to other memorials of the heroes too, and what is said concerning the pebbles: for along the shore they say there are pebbles of many colours, and the Greeks who dwell on the island say these took their colour from the scrapings the heroes made when they anointed themselves there; for, they relate, no such pebbles were seen either before that time or afterward.

They give clearer proofs still than these, that the sailing-out did not happen by way of the Symplegades, using the poet himself as witness for those places. For, showing forth the danger of the passage, he says it is not possible to sail past that place: "but the waves of the sea and the blasts of destructive fire carry along together the planks of ships and the bodies of men."

Now about the Cyanean rocks it is not said that fire is sent up, but about the strait that divides Sicily, on either side of which the fiery blasts lie, both the island itself burning continually, and the flow about Etna having often overrun the land.

div.head: The heroic cults of Tarentum
div.p: At Tarentum, at certain times, they say sacrifices are offered to the sons of Atreus, of Tydeus, of Aeacus, and of Laertes, and a sacrifice is performed separately for the descendants of Agamemnon on another special day, on which it is the custom for women not to taste of what is sacrificed to them. There is also, among them, a temple of Achilles.

It is said that after the Tarentines took possession, the place they now inhabit was called Heraclea, and in earlier times, when the Ionians held it, Pleion; and even before that, it is said to have been named Sigeum by the Trojans who then held it.

div.head: Philoctetes honoured among the Sybarites
div.p: Among the Sybarites, Philoctetes is said to be honoured. For, returning from Troy, he is said to have settled at the place called Mycalla, in the territory of Croton, said to lie a hundred and twenty stades away, and there, it is recorded, he dedicated the bow of Heracles in the temple of Apollo of the Sun.

From there, they say, the Crotoniates, upon gaining control of the region, dedicated it in their own temple of Apollo. It is said too that, dying there, he lies beside the river Sybaris, having gone to the aid of the Rhodians who came there with Tlepolemus and joined battle with the barbarian inhabitants of that country.

div.head: The shrine of Athena Hellenia at Metapontum
div.p: About the part of Italy called Gargaria, near Metapontum, they say there is a temple of Athena Hellenia, where the tools of Epeius are said to be dedicated, those he used to build the wooden horse, from which he gave it its name. For, appearing to him in a dream, Athena bade him dedicate the tools; and because of this, delayed in his departure, he was kept wandering in the place, unable to sail away; wherefore the temple is called that of Athena Hellenia.

div.head: The friendly dogs of the shrine of Athena Achaia
div.p: It is said that at the place called Daunia there is a temple of Athena Achaia, in which bronze axes and the arms of Diomedes' companions, and of Diomedes himself, are said to be dedicated. In this place, they say, there are dogs that do no harm to any Greeks who arrive, but fawn upon them as though upon their closest companions. All the Daunians and their neighbours dress in black, both men and women, for this reason, it seems.

For the Trojan women, taken captive and brought to those places, fearing they would suffer bitter slavery at the hands of the women already established there among the Achaeans, are said to have burned their ships, so that they might at once escape the slavery they expected, and, by forcing the men to remain with them, might, once reconciled, gain them as husbands. The poet has described them very well indeed; for they may be seen, it seems, trailing their robes and deep-bosomed.

div.head: The bronze antler dedicated by Diomedes
div.p: Among the Peucetians they say there is a temple of Artemis, in which there is dedicated a bronze antler renowned in those parts, bearing the inscription "Diomedes to Artemis." The myth is that he placed it about the neck of a deer, and that it grew fast there, and that it was later found in this state by Agathocles, king of the Sicilian Greeks, and dedicated by him in the temple of Zeus.

div.head: The saffron fields of Cape Pelorias
div.p: At the Sicilian headland called Pelorias, they say so much saffron grows that, while among some of the inhabitants of those parts the Greek flower is not even known, at Pelorias people bring down great wagons for it, and in the springtime make their bedding and their tents out of saffron.

div.head: The growing pool of Polycritus
div.p: Polycritus, who wrote the history of Sicily in verse, says that in a certain place inland there is a small pool, about the circumference of a shield, holding water that is clear, though a little turbid. If anyone in need of bathing steps into it, it grows wider; and if a second does too, it grows wider still; until at last it expands to hold as many as fifty men.

But once it has taken this number, it swells up again from its depths and casts the bodies of the bathers up and out onto the ground; and once this happens, it returns to its original circumference. This does not happen only with men, but if any four-footed creature steps in, the same thing occurs to it.

div.head: The fragrant mountain of Carthage and the spring of oil
div.p: In the territory of the Carthaginians they say there is a mountain called Uranion, full of every kind of timber, and adorned with many flowers, so that the surrounding regions, sharing in its fragrance over a great distance, offer travellers a most pleasant breath of air. Near this place, they say, there is a spring of oil, its smell like that of the shavings of cedar. They say that whoever approaches it must be ritually pure, and, this being so, the oil wells up the more abundantly, so that it may be drawn safely.

div.head: The fire-and-ice rock near the spring of oil
div.p: They say too that near this spring there is a great natural rock. This rock, they say, in summer sends up a flame of fire, but when winter comes, sprays from the same place a jet of water so cold that it is in no way different from snow. And they say this is not hidden, nor visible only briefly, but the fire rises the whole summer, and the water the whole winter.

div.head: The unquenchable burning stones of Thrace
div.p: It is said too that about the territory of the Sinti and the Maedi in Thrace there is a river called Pontus, in which certain stones are carried down that burn, and behave in the opposite way to charcoal made from wood; for, when fanned, they are quickly quenched, but when sprinkled with water, they flare up and burn better. When burning, they give off a smell like asphalt, so foul and pungent that no reptile can endure to remain in the place while they burn.

div.head: The lethal barley of Thrace
div.p: They say too that there is a place among them, not too small, about twenty stades, that bears barley which men use, but which horses and oxen refuse to eat, nor will any other animal. And no swine nor dog dares taste the dung of men who have eaten cake or bread made from this barley, for they die of it.

div.head: The healing spring of Scotussa in Thessaly
div.p: At Scotussa in Thessaly they say there is a small spring, from which flows water that quickly heals wounds and bruises, both of men and of pack animals; and if one places a piece of wood into it that has been split but not entirely broken apart, it grows together again and returns to its original state.

div.head: The boy hunters and their hawks in Thrace
div.p: About Thrace, above Amphipolis, they say something occurs that is marvellous and hard to believe for those who have not seen it. For the boys, going out from the villages and the nearby places to hunt small birds, take hawks along with them to hunt together, and they do it in this way.

When they come to a suitable place, they call the hawks by name, shouting; and the hawks, when they hear the boys' voices, come and drive the birds toward them; and the birds, afraid of the hawks, flee into the bushes, where the boys, striking with sticks, catch them. What one would most marvel at of all is this: when the hawks themselves catch one of the birds, they throw it down to the hunters, and the boys, giving the hawks a portion of everything caught, go away.

div.head: The jackdaws and the Enetian offering
div.p: A marvel is said to occur among the Enetians too. For onto their land there often descend countless myriads of jackdaws, which, once the people have sown their crops, devour them; and so the Enetians, before the birds are about to descend, set out gifts on the borders of their land, scattering seeds of every kind of fruit, and if the jackdaws taste of these, they do not cross over into the land, and the Enetians know they will be at peace; but if they do not taste of them, the people expect it as though an enemy's invasion were coming upon them.

div.head: The beetle-graveyard of Chalcidice
div.p: In Chalcidice, near Olynthus in Thrace, they say there is a place called "the beetles' destruction," a little larger than a threshing-floor, into which, when any other animal comes, it goes away again; but of the beetles that come there, not one does, but they wander round the place in a circle and die of hunger.

div.head: The lethal spring of the Thracian Cyclopes
div.p: Among the Thracian Cyclopes there is a small spring, whose water is, to the eye, clear and transparent and just like other water, but when any animal drinks from it, it perishes at once.

div.head: The two-livered hares and the light of Dionysus
div.p: They say too that among the Crastonians, near the territory of the Bisaltae, the hares that are caught have two livers, and that there is a certain place, about a plethron in size, into which whatever animal enters dies.

There is also there another great and beautiful temple of Dionysus, in which, during the festival and the sacrifice, it is said that when the god is about to grant a good year, a great gleam of fire appears, seen by all who are gathered about the sanctuary; but when he portends a poor harvest, this light does not appear, but darkness holds the place as on any other night.

div.head: The self-filling cauldrons of Elis
div.p: In Elis they say there is a certain building, about eight stades from the city, into which, at the Dionysia, three empty bronze cauldrons are placed. Having done this, they invite any of the visiting Greeks who wishes to examine the vessels and to seal the doors of the building.

And when they are about to open it, having shown the seals to the citizens and to the strangers, they open it thus. Those who enter find the cauldrons full of wine, the floor and the walls undisturbed, so that no suspicion can be entertained that this is contrived by some trick. They say there are kites there too, which snatch meat from those carrying it through the marketplace, but do not touch what is set apart for sacrifice.

div.head: The moles that cannot live at Coronea
div.p: At Coronea in Boeotia they say moles cannot live there nor burrow in the ground, though the rest of Boeotia has a great abundance of them.

div.head: The swimming land-mice of Lusi
div.p: At Lusi in Arcadia they say there is a spring in which land-mice occur and swim, making their home there. The same thing is said to occur at Lampsacus too.

div.head: The two ravens of Crannon
div.p: At Crannon in Thessaly they say there are only two ravens in the whole city. When these raise young, it seems, they themselves depart, leaving behind just as many others born of them.

div.head: The eternal fire and bitumen of Apollonia
div.p: At Apollonia, which lies near the territory of the Atlantini, they say mined bitumen and pitch occur, springing up from the earth in the same way as springs of water, no different from the Macedonian kind, but blacker and thicker in nature. Not far from this place there is a fire that burns continually, as those who live in that country say.

The burning place is not large, it seems, but about the size of five couches. It smells of sulphur and alum, and around it there grows, remarkably, deep grass and great trees, not four cubits from the fire. It burns continually too about Lycia and about Megalopolis in the Peloponnese.

div.head: The prolific livestock of Illyria
div.p: It is said too that among the Illyrians the livestock give birth twice a year, and most bear twins, and many bear three or four kids, some even five or more, and readily give as much as three half-measures of milk. They say too that the hens there lay not once, as elsewhere, but two or three times a day.

div.head: The great wild oxen of Paeonia
div.p: It is said too that in Paeonia the wild oxen are by far the largest of all those among the other nations, and that their horns hold four choes, some even more.

div.head: The strait of Sicily and its terrifying waves
div.p: Concerning the strait of Sicily, many others have written, and this author too says a marvellous thing occurs. From the Tyrrhenian sea, the swell, borne with a great rushing sound, strikes against both headlands, that of Sicily and that of Italy called Rhegium, and, borne from the open sea into the narrows, is confined; and when this happens, it raises a wave aloft with a great roar, over a very great extent of its upward course, so that the rising is visible even to those far off, appearing not like an ordinary rise of the sea, but white and foaming, resembling the surge that occurs in the most overwhelming storms.

And sometimes the swells from both headlands crash together and cause a confluence incredible to describe and unbearable to behold; and sometimes, separating after their clash, they present so deep and dreadful a sight to those forced to watch that many cannot control themselves, but fall, their sight darkened by fear.

And when the wave, having struck against whichever place, and risen up to the heights, is carried down again into the sea flowing beneath, then again, with a great bellowing and with great swift whirlpools, the sea boils up and rises, churned from the depths, and changes through every kind of colour: now appearing dark, now deep blue, and often shot through with purple.

Its course and its length, and further its backward flow, no reptile endures to hear or to see, but all flee to the foothills nearby. And as the swell subsides, the whirlpools are borne aloft, making such varied convolutions that they seem to produce motions like the coiling of waterspouts or of some great serpents.

div.head: The bronze pillar of Deiope at Eleusis
div.p: They say that when the Athenians were building the temple of Demeter at Eleusis, a bronze pillar was found enclosed within the stones, on which was inscribed "this is the tomb of Deiope," whom some say was the wife of Musaeus, others the mother of Triptolemus.

div.head: The palms of the Aeolian islands
div.p: On one of the islands called those of Aeolus they say a great abundance of palm-trees grew, whence it is called Phoenicodes ("palm-island"). What is said by Callisthenes, then, would not be true, that the plant took its name from the Phoenicians of Syria who dwell along the coast.

But indeed some say that the Phoenicians themselves were so called by the Greeks because, being the first to sail the sea, they killed and slaughtered all whom they put ashore among; and in the language of the Perrhaebians, too, "to redden with blood" is phoinixai.

div.head: The ancient stele of the Ainianes
div.p: In the land called Ainiake, near the place called Hypata, an ancient stele is said to have been found, which the Ainianes, wishing to know whose it was, since it bore an inscription in ancient letters, sent certain men to carry to Athens.

As they journeyed through Boeotia, and conferred with some of the local people about their errand, they are said to have been brought into the place called the Ismenion at Thebes; for there, it was thought, the meaning of the letters' inscription might best be discovered, since there were dedicatory offerings there bearing letters of similarly ancient form. From these, it is said, comparing what was known to what was sought, they made out and wrote down the following verses.

"Heracles dedicated this precinct to Cythera Persephassa, driving the herds of Geryon and leading Erytheia; whom the goddess Pasiphaessa subdued with desire. To this son of mine, and to the wife of Erythus, nymph-born Erythe, I gave this ground as a memorial of friendship, beneath the shady oak."

By this inscription the place itself came to be called Erythus, and it was made clear that he led the cattle from there and not from Erytheia; for nowhere in the regions of Libya and Iberia, they say, is the name Erytheia to be found at all.

div.head: The dug salt of Utica in Libya
div.p: In Libya, at the place called Utica, which lies, they say, in the gulf between the Hermaean and the Hippian headlands, beyond Carthage some two hundred stades (which is said to have been founded by the Phoenicians two hundred and eighty-seven years before Carthage itself, as is recorded in the Phoenician histories), they say dug salt occurs, at a depth of three fathoms, white to the eye and not solid but like the stickiest gum; and when it is brought up into the sun, it hardens and becomes like Parian marble. From it, they say, little figures and other implements are carved.

div.head: The silver of Tartessus
div.p: It is said that the first of the Phoenicians who sailed to Tartessus brought back so much silver in exchange for the oil and other seafaring wares they had brought in, that they could no longer find room to take on the silver, but were compelled, as they sailed away from those parts, to make of silver all the other things they used, and indeed all their anchors too.

div.head: The great tunny of the Phoenicians of Gades
div.p: It is said that the Phoenicians who dwell at the place called Gades, sailing out beyond the Pillars of Heracles with an east wind for four days, arrive at certain desert places, full of reeds and seaweed, which, when the tide is out, are not submerged, but when the tide is in, are flooded over; there is found an extraordinary abundance of tunny, incredible in size and bulk, when they run aground there; these they salt and pack into vessels and carry off to Carthage. Of these alone the Carthaginians do not permit export, but, on account of their excellence in eating, consume them themselves.

div.head: The goat of Pedasa and the two ravens
div.p: In Pedasa in Caria a sacrifice is performed to Zeus, at which they send forth a certain goat, about which they say a marvellous thing occurs. Walking from Pedasa seventy stades through a great crowd of onlookers, it is neither disturbed in its course nor turns aside from the road, but goes ahead of the priest, though bound only by a cord. Marvellous too is this: that there are two ravens continually about the temple of Zeus there, and no other approaches the place, and one of the two has the front of its neck white.

div.head: The frozen spring-salt of the Illyrian Ardiaei
div.p: Among the Illyrians called Ardiaei, on the borders between them and the Autariatae, they say there is a great mountain, and near it a ravine, from which water leaps up, not at every season but in spring, in great abundance; this they gather, and keep by day under cover, and set out by night in the open air. And when they have done this for five or six days, the water freezes, and becomes the finest salt, which they keep chiefly for their livestock; for salt is not brought in to them, since they dwell far from the sea and have no dealings with others. For their livestock, then, they have the greatest need of it; for they salt them twice a year. And if they fail to do this, it happens that most of their livestock perish.

div.head: The locust that fights the scorpion
div.p: At Argos they say there occurs a kind of locust called "scorpion-fighter." As soon as it sees a scorpion, it stands against it, and the scorpion likewise against it. It runs around the scorpion in a circle, shrilling; and the scorpion, raising its sting, turns about with it in the same place, then little by little lowers its sting, until at last it is fully extended, the locust running round it all the while. At the last, the locust approaches and devours it. They say it is good, too, to eat this locust as a remedy for the sting of a scorpion.

div.head: The venomous wasps of Naxos
div.p: They say the wasps at Naxos, when they have eaten of a viper (for its flesh, it seems, is dear to them), whenever they then sting someone, cause such extreme pain that the sting seems worse than that of the vipers themselves.

div.head: The Scythian arrow-poison from vipers
div.p: They say the Scythian poison, with which they dip their arrows, is made from the viper. The Scythians, it seems, watch for vipers already carrying live young, and, taking them, let them rot for some days. When it seems to them sufficiently decomposed, they pour human blood into a small pot, bury it in dung, and seal it. When this too has putrefied, they mix the watery matter that settles above the blood with the venom of the viper, and so make it deadly.

div.head: The asp-like snake of Curium in Cyprus
div.p: At Curium in Cyprus they say there is a kind of snake with power like that of the Egyptian asp, except that in winter, if it bites, it has no effect, whether for some other reason, or because the creature becomes sluggish, frozen stiff by the cold, and altogether powerless, unless it is warmed.

div.head: The deadly thorn-tree of Ceos
div.p: At Ceos they say there is a certain kind of wild pear-tree, from whose thorn, if one is pricked, one dies.

div.head: The white bears of Mysia
div.p: In Mysia they say there is a kind of white bear, which, when hunted, emit such a breath that it rots the flesh of the dogs, and likewise of the other beasts, making it uneatable. And if anyone forces his way close to them, they let out from their mouths a great quantity of phlegm, it seems, which they blow into the faces of the dogs, and likewise of men, so as to choke and blind them.

div.head: The paralyzing hyena of Arabia
div.p: In Arabia they say there is a kind of hyena which, when it sees some beast, or a man steps upon its shadow, causes it to lose its voice and become rigid, unable to move its body. It does this to dogs too.

div.head: The lion-killer of Syria
div.p: In Syria, they say, there is a creature called the "lion-killer"; for the lion dies, it seems, when it eats of it. The lion does not do this willingly, however, but flees the creature; but when hunters catch it and roast it, and sprinkle it like white barley-meal over some other animal, and the lion tastes it, it is said to die at once. This creature harms the lion also if it merely urinates upon it.

div.head: Vultures and beetles killed by scent
div.p: It is said too that vultures die from the scent of perfume, if one anoints them or gives them something scented to eat. Beetles likewise die from the scent of roses.

div.head: The deadly geckos and flying mice
div.p: They say too that in Sicily and in Italy the geckos have a deadly bite, unlike ours, which are weak and mild. There is also a kind of flying mouse, whose bite causes death.

div.head: Snakes harmless to natives, harmful to strangers
div.p: In Mesopotamia of Syria, and at Istrus, they say certain small snakes occur, which do not bite the natives, but do great harm to strangers.

div.head: The vipers and dwellers of the Euphrates
div.p: About the Euphrates they say this happens completely: many are seen about the banks of the river, swimming across to either side, so that those observed there in the evening are seen the next morning on the other side; and those resting there do not bite the Syrians, but do not spare the Greeks.

div.head: The sacred snake of Thessaly
div.p: In Thessaly they say the snake called sacred destroys everyone, not only if it bites but even if it merely touches them. Wherefore, whenever it appears and its hiss is heard (though it appears rarely), both snakes and vipers and all the other beasts flee. In size it is not great, but middling. At Tenos, it is said, it was once killed in the city, in Thessaly, by a woman; and its death came about in this way.

A woman, drawing a circle and placing her drugs within it, stepped into the circle together with her son, and then imitated the creature's hiss; and it hissed back and drew near. As it sang, the woman fell asleep, and, as it drew still nearer, she was overcome and could not resist her sleep.

Her son, sitting beside her, struck her to wake her, at her bidding, and she had told him that if she fell fully asleep, both she and he would die, but if he forced her to rouse and drew the creature nearer, they would be saved. And when the snake reached the circle, it at once withered away.

div.head: The oath-water at Tyana
div.p: It is said that near Tyana there is a spring sacred to Zeus of Oaths (they call it Asbamaean); its water rises very cold, and bubbles like a cauldron. To those who swear truly it is sweet and gentle, but for those who swear falsely, justice follows swiftly at their heels. For it strikes at their eyes, their hands, and their feet; they are seized with dropsy and consumption, and cannot even leave the place beforehand, but remain there, lamenting beside the water, confessing what they have forsworn.

div.head: The sacred olive-shoot at Athens
div.p: At Athens they say the sacred shoot of the olive puts forth growth and becomes greater within a single day, and then quickly shrinks back again.

div.head: The pious sons saved from the lava of Etna
div.p: When the craters of Etna broke open and the lava poured over the land here and there like a torrent, the god honoured the race of the pious. For, overtaken by the flow because they carried their aged parents upon their shoulders to save them, the fiery stream, on drawing near them, split apart, turning its burning course aside, this way and that, and kept the young men unharmed together with their parents.

div.head: Pheidias's hidden self-portrait
div.p: It is said that the sculptor Pheidias, in fashioning the Athena on the Acropolis, impressed his own face upon the middle of her shield, and bound it fast to the statue by some hidden device, so that if anyone should wish to remove it, of necessity the whole statue would have to be taken apart and destroyed.

div.head: The statue that avenged Bitys of Argos
div.p: They say the statue of Bitys at Argos killed the man responsible for Bitys's death, falling upon him as he stood watching it. It would seem, then, that such things do not happen without purpose.

div.head: The dogs that turn back at the Black Mountains
div.p: They say the dogs pursue beasts only as far as the peaks of the mountains called the Black Mountains, but turn back whenever their pursuit brings them that far.

div.head: The white-leaved chastity-rod of the Phasis
div.p: In the river Phasis there grows a rod called "white-leaf," which jealous men, cutting it, throw about the maiden's chamber, and so keep the marriage undefiled.

div.head: The protective stone of the Tigris
div.p: In the Tigris, they say, there occurs a stone called, in the barbarian tongue, modon, quite white in colour; whoever holds it is harmed by no wild beast.

div.head: The fearless herb of the Scamander
div.p: In the Scamander, they say, there grows a plant called sistron, resembling a chickpea, with seeds that rattle, whence it took its name; those who hold it fear neither spirit nor any apparition.

div.head: The mad vine of Libya
div.p: About Libya there is a vine some call "the mad vine," whose fruit ripens some grapes, while others remain sour, and others are still in flower, and this for but a short time.

div.head: The devoted stone of Mount Sipylus
div.p: About Mount Sipylus, they say, there occurs a stone like a cylinder, which dutiful sons, when they find it, dedicate in the sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods, and never fall short in reverence, but remain forever devoted to their fathers.

div.head: The love-charm herb of Mount Taygetus
div.p: On Mount Taygetus there grows a plant called charisia, which women, at the beginning of spring, fasten about their necks, and are the more tenderly loved by men for it.

div.head: The colour-changing snakes of Mount Othrys
div.p: Othrys is a mountain of Thessaly, which bears the snakes called seps; these do not have a single colour, but always take on the likeness of the place they inhabit. Some of them have a colour like the land-snails of the earth; in others the scaly skin is greenish. Those that dwell among the sands take on the likeness of the sand in colour. Their bite produces thirst. Their bite is not rough or burning, but malignant.

div.head: The viper's deadly mating
div.p: When the dusky viper mates with the female viper, the female bites off his head during the union. For this reason, too, the young, as though avenging their father's death, tear open their mother's belly.

div.head: The dog-silencing stone of the Nile
div.p: In the river Nile, they say, there is produced a stone resembling a bean, at the sight of which dogs do not bark. It is of use, too, for those possessed by some spirit; for as soon as it is placed to their nostrils, the spirit departs.

div.head: The maddening "prudent" stone of the Maeander
div.p: In the river Maeander of Asia they say there is a stone called "prudent," by antiphrasis; whoever casts it into someone's bosom, that person becomes mad and kills one of his own kin.

div.head: The freezing of the Rhine and the Danube
div.p: The rivers Rhine and Danube flow beneath the Bear, the one passing the Germans, the other the Paeonians; in summer their current is navigable by ship, but in winter, frozen by the cold, they are ridden across on horseback as though over a plain.

div.head: The rivers of Thurii
div.p: About the city of Thurii they say there are two rivers, the Sybaris and the Crathis. The Sybaris makes those who drink of it timid, while the Crathis makes those who bathe in it fair-haired.

div.head: The wool-dyeing rivers of Euboea
div.p: In Euboea there are, they say, two rivers: from the one, which is called the Cerbes, the sheep that drink become white; the other, the Neleus, makes them black.

div.head: The eyesight herb of the Lycormas
div.p: By the river Lycormas there grows a plant resembling a spearhead, most excellent for dim-sightedness.

div.head: The periodic spring Arethusa at Syracuse
div.p: The spring called Arethusa at Syracuse in Sicily is said to be disturbed once every five years.

div.head: The madness-stone of the Berecynthian mountain
div.p: On the Berecynthian mountain there is produced, they say, a stone called "the knife"; whoever finds it, when the mysteries of Hecate are being celebrated, becomes mad, as Eudoxus says.

div.head: The colour-changing stone of Mount Tmolus
div.p: On Mount Tmolus, they say, there occurs a stone resembling pumice, which changes colour four times in a day; it is seen by maidens who have not yet come to full understanding through age.

div.head: The bellowing golden bull of Artemis Orthosia
div.p: On the altar of Artemis Orthosia there stands a golden bull, which, when hunters enter, sends forth a bellow.

div.head: The dim-sighted, locust-eating moles of Aetolia
div.p: Among the Aetolians they say the moles see but dimly, and do not eat earth but locusts.

div.head: The two-year pregnancy of elephants
div.p: They say the elephants carry their young for two years, though others say eighteen months, and have difficult labour at the birth.

div.head: Demaratus and his silent illness
div.p: Demaratus, a pupil of Timaeus of Locri, is said to have fallen ill and become speechless for ten days; on the eleventh, slowly recovering his senses from this derangement, he said that of all his life, that time had been the most pleasant to him.
